claims.text: Complex VR scenes exceed the efficient real-time rendering capacity of current devices, and delayed rendering can make displayed content inconsistent with user interaction, causing discomfort.

evidence_excerpts: The source explains that foveated rendering performs high-quality rendering in the foveal region and low-quality rendering in the peripheral region, allowing rendering to speed up without sacrificing perceived visual quality.
claims.text: Foveated rendering can accelerate rendering by giving the foveal region high quality and the peripheral region lower quality while preserving perceived visual quality.

claims.text: Visual acuity models and contrast sensitivity models are the two representative perceptual-model families used to guide foveated rendering quality allocation.

evidence_items.excerpt: The introduction reports that rendering overhead continues to increase in VR because of diversified surface materials, more dynamic objects, and more complex physical phenomena, then cites Potter et al. for an approximately 13 ms visual-latency tolerance threshold for the human visual system.
evidence_items.overview: This is a concrete motivation for foveated rendering: the technique is not presented merely as an optimization preference, but as a response to a perceptual timing constraint in VR. The 13 ms value bounds the performance problem, while the discussion of scene complexity explains why conventional full-quality rendering struggles to satisfy that bound.
evidence_items.title: VR Latency Tolerance Constraint

evidence_items.excerpt: The survey explains that approximately half of optic nerve fibers are distributed in the fovea and the rest across the periphery, then describes foveated rendering as high-quality rendering in the foveal region and low-quality rendering in the peripheral region.
evidence_items.overview: This passage supplies the perceptual mechanism behind the acceleration claim. It connects retinal resource distribution to an engineering strategy: spend rendering work where the user can perceive fine detail and reduce work in peripheral regions where lower fidelity is less noticeable.
evidence_items.title: Fovea-Periphery Quality Allocation

evidence_items.excerpt: The paper states that three challenges must be addressed in foveated rendering: using human-visual-system perceptual models, rendering different regions with different qualities, and integrating foveated rendering into existing rendering paradigms to improve rendering performance.
evidence_items.overview: This formal framing gives the survey its argumentative structure. It distinguishes perceptual modeling, regional quality assignment, and rendering-system integration as separate design obligations rather than treating foveated rendering as a single algorithmic trick.
evidence_items.title: Three Foveation Challenges

evidence_items.excerpt: The survey identifies visual acuity and contrast sensitivity as representative perceptual models for foveated rendering; it further divides visual acuity models into fall-off, binocular horopter, and ocular dominance models and lists spatial, spatio-temporal, spatio-luminance, spatio-chromatic, and critical-flicker-fusion contrast sensitivity functions.
evidence_items.overview: This evidence establishes why foveated rendering is a perceptual systems problem. The named model families define where visual fidelity can be reduced, which kinds of errors matter, and how spatial, temporal, luminance, and chromatic variation can become rendering constraints.
evidence_items.title: Visual Acuity and CSF Models

evidence_items.excerpt: The taxonomy section states that current foveated rendering methods are classified according to required input data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm; Table 2 then enumerates elements for those dimensions, including image/video, volume data, geometric meshes, point cloud, hologram data, light field, multi-resolution principles, LoD, and multiple rendering paradigms.
evidence_items.overview: This table evidence supports the survey's core organizing contribution. It makes the taxonomy operational by listing dimensions and categories that can be used to compare prior work and to guide new method design across data representations and renderer architectures.
evidence_items.title: Three-Dimensional Taxonomy Table

evidence_items.excerpt: Table 3 is introduced as a summary of foveated rendering technique implementations and the surrounding text says it classifies 90 published reports from 1990 to 2021 according to the three taxonomy dimensions, while also marking surveys, patents, and cutting-edge equipment.
evidence_items.overview: This evidence shows that the taxonomy is applied to a substantial body of literature rather than left as a conceptual proposal. The count and date range support the survey's claim to broad historical coverage across early and more recent foveated rendering work.
evidence_items.title: Ninety Reports Classified

evidence_items.excerpt: The discussion reviews FSNR, FWQI, FMSE, and WSSIM as objective quality metrics, then notes limitations: FSNR may miss perception, FWQI omits spatio-temporal CSF, FMSE assumes centered fixations, WSSIM depends on saliency-model choice, and no general accepted metric yet exists.
evidence_items.overview: This evidence grounds one of the survey's key open problems. It shows that evaluating foveated output is difficult because existing metrics each encode restrictive assumptions, which complicates comparison among methods and motivates better datasets and objective measures.
evidence_items.title: Foveated Metric Limitations

evidence_items.excerpt: The discussion identifies opportunities in using more HVS features such as visual masking, applying computer vision and AI for gaze prediction and reconstruction, improving foveated methods for hologram data and light fields, adapting nontrivial rendering paradigms for effects such as global illumination and caustics, and extending foveated rendering to AR and task assistance.
evidence_items.overview: This evidence consolidates the survey's practical interpretation. It identifies where the field remains underspecified: perceptual modeling, machine-learning assistance, emerging data types, renderer integration, AR display constraints, and foveated rendering as a tool for tasks beyond speed alone.
evidence_items.title: Future Research Opportunity Set

relations.rationale: The latency and scene-complexity problem explains why foveated rendering's perceptual acceleration strategy is valuable.
Visual acuity and contrast sensitivity models justify allocating higher quality to the fovea and lower quality to the periphery.
The three-dimensional taxonomy elaborates the survey's three design problems into classifiable method dimensions.
Classifying 90 reports demonstrates that the taxonomy can organize a broad literature sample.
The breadth of current principles and paradigms is closely related to the breadth of open research problems.

sections.body: The survey begins from a concrete systems pressure: VR applications require real-time responses while scenes become more expensive to render. The 13 ms latency tolerance and the observation that delayed content can conflict with user interaction ground the problem in perception rather than only hardware throughput. This makes foveated rendering a practical response to a user-experience constraint.
sections.heading: Performance Motivation

sections.body: The core mechanism is asymmetric human visual sensitivity. The source explains that the fovea supports clear central vision, while peripheral regions can tolerate reduced quality. Visual acuity and contrast sensitivity models turn that biological fact into rendering rules, indicating where spatial, temporal, luminance, or chromatic detail can be reduced with limited perceptual cost.
sections.heading: Perceptual Mechanism

sections.body: The paper does not treat foveated rendering as one technique. It frames the area as a combination of perceptual modeling, multi-quality regional rendering, and integration into renderer architectures. This framing is useful because a method can fail by using the wrong perception model, by choosing poor quality falloff, or by being incompatible with the rendering pipeline it is supposed to accelerate.
sections.heading: Three Design Problems

sections.body: The taxonomy is the survey's organizing contribution. By classifying methods by data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm, it connects design decisions to implementation contexts. The categories also prevent overly narrow comparisons: a technique for mesh rasterization, volume ray casting, hologram phase retrieval, or 360-degree video transmission may all be foveated, but they solve different engineering problems.
sections.heading: Taxonomy Contribution

sections.body: The application of the taxonomy to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021 gives the survey more than a conceptual structure. It functions as a map of the literature, separating early approaches from the more recent decade and showing how methods diversified across data representations, principles, and renderer types as hardware and application needs changed.
sections.heading: Historical Coverage

sections.body: The source is careful about evaluation limits. Existing objective metrics such as FSNR, FWQI, FMSE, and WSSIM each omit or assume important perceptual factors, such as spatio-temporal contrast sensitivity, fixation position, or saliency-model accuracy. That means performance gains alone are not enough; comparability depends on better perceptual metrics and datasets.
sections.heading: Limits and Assumptions

sections.body: For designers, the practical message is that foveated rendering should be chosen and evaluated as a system-level tradeoff among perception, data representation, rendering algorithm, display hardware, and task. The open problems around AR fusion, holograms, light fields, gaze prediction, AI reconstruction, and task guidance suggest that the field remains active even where core VR mesh and volume concepts are mature.
sections.heading: Practical Interpretation

source_dossier.summary_long: The source is a broad survey of foveated rendering, centered on the idea that VR and related interactive graphics systems cannot simply render every part of every scene at maximum quality when scene complexity and human latency tolerance are both severe constraints. The paper motivates the field with the increasing cost of rendering diverse materials, dynamic objects, and complex physical phenomena, and with the approximately 13 ms visual-latency tolerance discussed in its introduction. Against that background, foveated rendering is presented as a perceptual allocation strategy: render the foveal region at high quality, render peripheral regions at lower quality, and rely on human visual-system limits so that the user does not perceive unacceptable loss. The survey's argument is structured around three problems that any foveated method must solve: it must use an appropriate perceptual model, decide how quality varies across regions, and fit that decision into a concrete rendering paradigm. The perceptual discussion emphasizes visual acuity and contrast sensitivity models, including spatial, temporal, luminance, chromatic, and binocular considerations. The taxonomy then turns those concerns into a practical classification with three axes: input data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm. This lets the paper compare work on image/video, volumes, meshes, point clouds, holograms, and light fields, as well as principles such as multi-spatial resolution, multi-temporal resolution, multi-luminance resolution, multi-color resolution, and level of detail. The rendering-paradigm axis includes rasterization, ray tracing, ray casting, instant radiosity, shadow mapping, simplification, neural rendering, photon mapping, phase retrieval, and data transmission. By applying the taxonomy to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021, the survey presents the field as mature in some areas, especially volume data and geometric meshes, but still unresolved in others. Its discussion highlights open problems in broader use of human visual features, AI-assisted gaze and reconstruction methods, emerging data types such as holograms and light fields, objective quality metrics, AR fusion constraints, and task-oriented uses beyond speed improvement alone.
source_dossier.summary_short: This survey presents foveated rendering as a response to the real-time burden of complex VR scenes and the perceptual consequences of latency. It explains how human visual-system models let renderers concentrate fidelity near gaze while reducing work in peripheral regions. Its main contribution is a taxonomy organized by data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm, applied to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021.

summary: Wang, Shi, and Liu survey foveated rendering as a perceptually grounded acceleration strategy for VR and related display systems. The source frames the field around HVS perceptual models, regional quality variation, and integration into rendering paradigms, then proposes a three-dimensional taxonomy and applies it to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021.
